overview: Malawi’s regional history includes rock paintings, shared meals and skills learned through practice. Evidence comes from archaeological sites and from living communities whose traditions differ across the country.

periods.title: Nyasaland under British rule
periods.summary: The territory shown as Malawi on this map was then the Nyasaland Protectorate. That colonial name had been adopted in 1907. The map’s 1920 starting point is neither the beginning of local settlement nor the date of independence.

periods.title: Federation and the approach to independence
periods.summary: Nyasaland joined Northern and Southern Rhodesia in a federation in 1953. The federation dissolved in 1963, and Nyasaland became independent as Malawi the following July. Dissolution and independence were separate events.

periods.title: Independent Malawi
periods.summary: Malawi became independent on 6 July 1964. The United States recognised the new country that day and raised its consulate in Blantyre to embassy status. The republic and presidency followed in 1966.

periods.title: The republic under Banda
periods.summary: Malawi became a republic on 6 July 1966, with Hastings Kamuzu Banda as president. His government ruled through a one-party system. The later movement for multiparty politics challenged that political order without ending Malawi’s independence.

periods.title: A referendum changes the political path
periods.summary: In June 1993, voters chose a multiparty political system in a national referendum. Constitutional changes then allowed opposition parties to organise legally. Parliamentary and presidential elections followed in May 1994.

periods.title: Multiparty elections and a new government
periods.summary: The elections of 17 May 1994 brought a change of leadership. Bakili Muluzi defeated Banda in the presidential contest and was inaugurated on 21 May. The republic continued under a different government and political framework.

periods.title: Recognition for a living dance tradition
periods.summary: Tchopa joined UNESCO’s Representative List in 2014. The Lhomwe tradition combines performance with learning and mutual support, including help for community members facing illness, bereavement or heavy farm work.

periods.title: Knowledge around the shared meal
periods.summary: UNESCO recognised the culinary tradition of nsima in 2017. This recognition concerns the knowledge of preparing and sharing food, including learning within families; it is not the date the dish was invented.

sections.title: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack

items.text: At Chongoni, red rock paintings include circles, radiating lines and other geometric patterns made with red oxide pigment. Researchers associate this earlier tradition with hunter-gatherers. Suggested links with rainmaking are interpretations, rather than translations of a known written code. A circle on a rock does not come with its original caption.

Later Chongoni paintings used white clay for animal-like and other figures. Many are linked with Chewa women’s ceremonies, and painting continued into the twentieth century. Excavations also recovered hunted-animal bones around two thousand years old. Researchers warn that these finds are difficult to connect with particular paintings: dating a meal’s remains does not automatically date the art nearby.

sections.title: Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe

items.text: Nsima is a thick porridge made with maize flour, and its name also refers to a wider culinary tradition. UNESCO’s account follows the work from growing and storing maize through pounding, preparing accompaniments and serving. The finished bowl is only the last stage of a much longer chain of skills.

Sharing nsima provides an occasion for families to spend time together. Children learn food skills from adults through practice, while recipes, schoolbooks and festivals offer other ways to pass on the tradition. Learning dinner can involve both a book and watching someone who already knows what to do.

sections.title: The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack

items.text: In Tchopa, a Lhomwe performance from southern Malawi, dancers move in a circle and cross one another’s paths to drums of three sizes. Some carry packs containing farming tools, animal skins, puppets or old kitchen utensils. The equipment links performance with work and everyday objects. Getting ready for this dance can involve more than finding your shoes.

Tchopa knowledge passes through rehearsals and performances, with children increasingly joining older practitioners. The group also has roles for costume makers, drum makers and musicians. UNESCO describes members helping one another during bereavement or illness and sharing farm labour when someone is overburdened. The relationships continue after the dancing stops.

Vimbuza is a healing tradition associated with Tumbuka communities in northern Malawi. UNESCO describes people staying in a healer’s village house, with singing, drumming and dance forming part of their care. Women and children gather around the person receiving the ritual. This account records cultural understandings of illness and spiritual help, and shows care involving a wider community. It does not establish that the ritual cures an illness.

sections.title: A university begins in a former school

items.text: The University of Malawi began teaching on 29 September 1965 with ninety students in Blantyre, using a former secondary-school campus. Its institutional establishment had come in 1964. The small first intake helps make a large institution’s beginning easier to picture: a university can start with a group of learners before it develops several campuses and colleges.

The university’s history records Kamuzu College of Nursing joining as a constituent college in September 1979, followed by a College of Medicine in Blantyre in 1991. These institutions made training nurses and doctors part of the university’s work. The dates describe that institutional history, rather than when Malawians first practised healing or cared for sick relatives.

sections.title: Pupils who asked for better toilets

items.text: A 2024 UNICEF report describes the water, sanitation and hygiene club at Mbande Primary School in Karonga. Its student chairperson, Gladson Kaunda, said members met on Mondays and pressed the school committee for more toilets and spaces for adolescent girls. They received supplies including buckets and soap. Pupils were helping shape their school environment as well as learning in it.

At Mkazomba Primary School in Lilongwe, a 2024 UNICEF report describes a solar-powered water system with storage tanks, taps and handwashing facilities. Pupils had previously walked to a village well to fetch water. Water nearer their classrooms also helped with cleaning toilets, and local community members received maintenance training. Keeping a school running involves pipes and practical skills as well as lessons.

ending.text: British rule ended when Nyasaland became independent Malawi on 6 July 1964. The country became a republic in 1966 and continued through the change from Banda’s rule to multiparty government in 1994. The map’s earlier start date does not make Malawi independent in 1920, and changes of government did not end its communities.
